questions.q: What were the starting years of planned development for India, Pakistan, and China, and what common planning instrument did all three adopt?
questions.a: India (1951), Pakistan (1956), China (1953) — all adopted Five Year Plans. A wrong answer (e.g., saying India started in 1947 or China in 1949) reveals confusion between political independence/establishment and the formal commencement of planned economic development, missing that planning is a policy choice distinct from sovereignty.

questions.q: Why does the textbook state that China's reforms in 1978 were "on its own initiative" while India and Pakistan's reforms were "forced upon" them by international agencies?
questions.a: China's leadership voluntarily initiated reforms due to dissatisfaction with slow growth under Maoism (per capita grain output in 1978 equaled mid-1950s levels), whereas India (1991) and Pakistan (1988) faced balance-of-payments crises requiring IMF/World Bank loans with structural adjustment conditionalities. A wrong answer attributing China's reforms to external pressure reveals misunderstanding of the distinction between endogenous vs exogenous reform triggers — a critical concept for evaluating reform sustainability.

questions.q: Using Table 8.1, calculate how many years it would take for Pakistan's population to double at its 2021-23 annual growth rate of 1.96%, and compare with China's -0.10% rate. What does this imply for future dependency ratios?
questions.a: Pakistan doubling time = 70/1.96 ≈ 35.7 years (Rule of 70). China's negative growth means population shrinking — no doubling. Implication: Pakistan faces rising youth dependency burden needing massive job creation; China faces rising elderly dependency with shrinking workforce. A wrong calculation (e.g., using 72/1.96 or ignoring negative sign) or missing the dependency ratio implication shows inability to translate demographic data into economic policy challenges.

questions.q: Table 8.3 shows China's industry sector employs 32% of workforce but contributes 38% to GVA, while India's industry employs 26% but contributes 28%. Calculate and compare the labour productivity ratios (GVA share / workforce share) for industry in both countries. What does the difference reveal about industrial structure?
questions.a: China industry productivity ratio = 38/32 = 1.1875. India industry productivity ratio = 28/26 = 1.0769. China's higher ratio indicates more capital-intensive, higher-value manufacturing (SOE reform, township-village enterprises, SEZs), while India's lower ratio suggests more labour-intensive, lower-value industrial activity. A wrong answer reversing the ratio or missing the structural interpretation shows inability to derive productivity insights from sectoral share data.

questions.q: Evaluate the textbook's claim that China's human development gains (Table 8.5) were "attributed not to the reform process but the strategies that China adopted in the pre-reform period." Use two specific indicators from Table 8.5 to support your evaluation.
questions.a: Strong evaluation: China's life expectancy (78.0) and infant mortality (4.8) far exceed India (72.0, 25.5) and Pakistan (67.6, 51). These reflect pre-1978 investments: commune-based rural health (barefoot doctors), universal primary education, land reforms ensuring food security. Post-1978 growth accelerated income (GNI $22,029 vs India $9,047) but HDI foundations were laid earlier. A weak answer crediting only post-1978 growth misses the textbook's explicit causal distinction — a common board exam trap.

questions.q: Construct a comparative timeline (1947-2024) showing three parallel tracks: political system evolution, reform initiation year, and one key policy milestone per decade for each country. Identify one critical juncture where paths diverged most sharply.
questions.a: Good answer includes: India (democracy throughout, 1991 reforms, 1950s land reforms/1960s Green Revolution/1991 LPG), Pakistan (military coups 1958, 1977, 1999, 1988 reforms, 1960s Green Revolution/1970s nationalization/1980s denationalization), China (one-party throughout, 1978 reforms, 1950s land reform/1958 GLF/1978 HRS). Critical juncture: 1978 — China reforms while India/Pakistan wait 10-13 more years. Poor answer lists events without analytical framing or misses the 1978 divergence.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Comparative development analysis is the systematic examination of economic and human development ______ across countries using standardized indicators (GDP growth, sectoral composition, demographic trends, HDI components) to identify how differing political systems, policy choices, and initial conditions produce divergent outcomes over time.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're at a family dinner where three cousins — born the same year — share their life stories: one became a doctor (China), one an engineer (India), one struggled with unstable jobs (______).
What is Comparative development analysis? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Comparative development analysis is the systematic examination of economic and human development trajectories across countries using standardized indicators (GDP growth, sectoral composition, demographic trends, HDI components) to identify how differing political systems, policy choices, and initial conditions produce divergent outcomes.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: That's exactly what this chapter does with India, Pakistan, and China — all starting planned development around ______.
What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Comparative development analysis?
questions.a: Students believe China's higher GDP growth (Table 8.2) is solely due to post-1978 market reforms, ignoring that China's pre-1978 investments in human capital (health, education, land equity) created the *capacity* for that growth.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can interpret comparative data tables (demographic, GDP, sectoral, HDI) to explain why China outperformed India and Pakistan on growth and human development despite similar starting points, and can articulate the role of political system and reform timing in shaping these divergences.
